newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac declares armed truce with Jospin.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac declares armed truce with Jospin.

text.p: Conservative French President Jacques Chirac declared an armed truce with his Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin on Monday, vowing vigilance to ensure France meets the terms for a single European currency.
In his first television interview since being shorn of much of his power by a left-wing victory in parliamentary elections, Chirac said he wanted "constructive cohabitation" with Jospin.
He expected power-sharing would run its full course until new presidential and parliamentary elections in 2002 if the government elected last month did not spark a crisis.

But he criticised Jospin's policies on privatisation, layoffs, nuclear power and immigration and said France must control public spending to meet the criteria for European economic and monetary union.
Chirac said the planned 1999 launch date and the agreed conditions for a single European currency must be respected.
"It would have very serious conquences for France not to do it -- very, very serious -- we would isolate ourselves," he said.
He said this year's public deficit was running at about 3.5 percent of gross domestic product, but France could achieve the Maastricht Treaty target of three percent if it held down spending.

"The parliamentary majority has been elected for five years. It is up to the government to act in such a way that no crisis occurs which could call that contract into question," Chirac said in the 75-minute live Bastille Day TV interview.

Asked whether he expected such a crisis, he said: "I do not wish that." And asked whether he expected the legislature would run its full term, the president, who has the right to dissolve parliament after it has sat for one year, said: "I think so."

Chirac sought to mark out a broad role for himself, going far beyond the traditional presidential domains of defence and foreign affairs into maintaining social cohesion and upholding France's high-technology industries and scientific research.

The centre-right's June 1 defeat, in an election called 10 months early by Chirac, plunged France into its third bout of left-right power-sharing in 11 years, raising fears of paralysis at a time of economic stagnation and near-record unemployment.
But the president, looking relaxed and self-confident, said he did not regret having dissolved parliament because the country had been in "a crisis of immobility".
He also said he did not favour reducing the presidential term to five years from seven.

While stressing his personal relations with Jospin were courteous, the Gaullist head of state criticised several of the government's policies, hitting hardest at its unpopular decision to legalise thousands of mainly African immigrants who had been in legal limbo.

"It would be an encouragement (to illegal immigrants). The employment and social situation does not allow our country to do this...and it would feed those xenophobic and racist reactions which I hate," Chirac said.
He criticised as "obsolete and absurd" government plans to revive a requirement for state labour inspectors to authorise all layoffs by private companies, scrapped in 1986.
And he warned the government it could slam the door to European alliances if it kept control of commercial companies such as defence electronics giant Thomson-CSF.

Three days after Jospin decided to halt the privatisation of Thomson-CSF and retain a decisive state shareholding, Chirac said: "The state today no longer has any place in the management of competitive industries.

"Our big companies cannot live without alliances and especially European alliances...and modern countries cannot imagine their private companies teaming up with public companies subject to considerations that have nothing to do with the market," he said.
